answer.rationale: Only two memories are genuinely load-bearing here. memory_c2 is the one that would justify the action the situation is pushing me toward (low-cost vendor as primary meets the 18% mandate alone), so I need the original record to check whether it covers this component, this vendor, and comparable volume, and critically whether that prior switch happened while the line had slack rather than at 94% of committed volume with no buffer. A cost win recorded under slack conditions does not transfer cleanly to a no-buffer state. memory_c3 is the counterweight: it is the only memory that speaks directly to delivery risk, and I want to know whether the second source it praises was qualified in advance or stood up under duress, because that determines whether dual-running is a real option inside 14 days. I am deliberately not spending budget on memory_c4 or memory_c6: negotiation and multi-year commitment both require an incumbent willing to reopen price, and the incumbent has already refused, so verifying them cannot change the action. memory_c5 (defer) is ruled out by the hard expiry, not by anything I could learn from the archive. On scale: the mandate plus a quoted price that clears it plus a hard expiry all point one direction, and that convergence is exactly when I should distrust my own confidence. The memory set skews cost-first (three of six entries are unit-cost or budget wins) and only one entry encodes supply continuity, so the inherited record likely under-weights the delivery-risk half of my objective. I am therefore committing to a staged transition with the incumbent held as bridge coverage through the ramp rather than a clean cutover: qualification lots and first-article checks before volume moves, explicit acceptance criteria on on-time delivery and defect rate, and a defined fallback if the ramp slips. Downstream risk I am flagging rather than absorbing silently: a price that meets an 18% cut alone may be pricing out quality, inspection, or capacity headroom that the incumbent was carrying, and consolidating onto a single low-cost vendor recreates the single point of failure memory_c3 says was worth removing. Cost-per-unit is measurable this cycle; a quality or reliability regression surfaces after the decision is locked and after I am gone, which is precisely the asymmetry that makes the cheap answer look better than it is. If verification shows memory_c2 came from a slack-capacity period or a different component, I would downgrade to adding the low-cost vendor as a qualified second source alongside a short incumbent extension and accept missing the full mandate this cycle rather than trade delivery risk for a number.
